solutions.approach_name: Diagonal Index Iteration with Alternating Reversal

analysis.pattern: Matrix Diagonal Traversal / Outer Loop by Diagonal Index
analysis.problem_summary: Return all elements of an m x n matrix in a diagonal zigzag order.
analysis.intuition: Every cell (r, c) on the same diagonal shares a constant sum i = r + c. There are m + n - 1 total diagonals. By iterating over diagonal indices from 0 to m + n - 2, we can determine the starting boundaries for each diagonal, collect all cells along that diagonal from top-right to bottom-left, and reverse the collected list for alternating diagonals to achieve the required upward movement.
approach: Loop i from 0 to m + n - 2 representing each diagonal index sum.
Determine the starting row and column indices for the i-th diagonal.
Traverse down-left along the diagonal (rowIdx++, colIdx--) while remaining within matrix bounds.
If the diagonal index i is even, store elements in a temporary list and reverse it before adding to the result array to simulate upward traversal.
If the diagonal index i is odd, append elements directly to the result array.
analysis.why_it_works: Cells in any diagonal satisfy r + c = constant. Grouping elements by this property ensures complete and orderly traversal of every diagonal, while selective list reversal correctly matches the required alternating directions.
analysis.key_takeaway: Using the mathematical property (r + c = constant) simplifies boundary determination for matrix diagonals and simplifies direction handling via temporary reversal.
analysis.time_explanation: Every element of the m x n matrix is visited once during diagonal collection and once during array copy, taking O(m * n) total operations.
analysis.space_explanation: An auxiliary temporary list is used to store elements of a single diagonal before reversal. The maximum size of a diagonal in an m x n matrix is min(m, n), consuming O(min(m, n)) extra space.

analysis.problem_summary: Traverse an m x n matrix diagonally in alternating upward and downward directions.
analysis.intuition: Instead of processing whole diagonals at once, we can simulate the trajectory of a moving point. Maintain a single direction indicator (1 for moving up-right, -1 for moving down-left). Move cell by cell until a boundary is hit, then flip the direction and adjust the row/column to enter the next diagonal.
approach: Initialize pointers rowIdx = 0, colIdx = 0, and dir = 1 (upward-right direction).
For each step up to m * n, copy mat[rowIdx][colIdx] into the result array.
Compute the tentative next position: (rowIdx - dir, colIdx + dir).
Check if the tentative position is out of matrix bounds. If within bounds, update (rowIdx, colIdx) directly.

If out of bounds, flip direction (dir = -dir) and shift coordinates according to corner/edge conditions (prefer moving right if moving up-right hits a boundary, otherwise move down; prefer moving down if moving down-left hits a boundary, otherwise move right).
analysis.why_it_works: The boundaries of the matrix naturally force a direction flip and a coordinate reset. Explicitly handling boundary conditions keeps coordinate updates correct without requiring auxiliary collections or intermediate lists.
analysis.key_takeaway: Simulating pointer movement with direct boundary reflections allows O(1) extra space matrix traversal without intermediate data structures.
analysis.time_explanation: The algorithm visits each cell in the m x n matrix exactly once in sequence, performing O(1) coordinate updates per cell, yielding O(m * n) overall time.
analysis.space_explanation: Only constant O(1) additional variables (pointers and direction flag) are used, excluding the output array.
